interviewQuestions.question: What does 'superscalar' mean, and why don't processors just keep going wider (8-wide, 16-wide)?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define superscalar as the ability to fetch, decode, and issue more than one instruction per cycle, achieved by duplicating front-end and execution hardware — multiple decoders, multiple ALUs, multiple issue ports — as opposed to a scalar pipeline's hard ceiling of one instruction per cycle no matter how fast the clock runs.

Going wider stops paying off for two compounding reasons. First, **available ILP**: real programs don't reliably offer N genuinely independent, ready-to-issue instructions every single cycle — dependence chains, branches, and irregular memory access mean the *actual* exploitable parallelism in typical code plateaus well below what an arbitrarily wide machine could theoretically consume, so a wider front end increasingly just sits underutilized. Second, **structural cost that grows faster than linearly**: issue logic has to check dependencies between every pair of candidate instructions being considered for simultaneous issue, which is roughly a quadratic problem in issue width; register file read/write ports, bypass/forwarding networks, and wakeup logic all scale up superlinearly too, eating power and die area far faster than the extra throughput they buy.

Concrete consequence: mainstream cores plateaued around 4-8-wide issue for exactly this reason, and instead pushed further gains into deeper reorder buffers (exploiting ILP across a wider *window* of the program, not a wider single cycle) and better branch prediction (reducing how often speculative work gets thrown away) rather than continuing to widen raw issue.

**Testing:** naming both limiting factors — program-inherent ILP scarcity and superlinear hardware cost — as a ceiling on width, not just one of them.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why issue width plateaus

interviewQuestions.question: What hardware changes when you go from a scalar to a superscalar pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd walk through the front end and back end separately, since both need duplication for width to actually help.

The **front end** needs to fetch multiple instruction words per cycle instead of one — wider fetch bandwidth from the instruction cache, and parallel decoders decoding several instructions simultaneously rather than one decoder running N times. The **execution back end** needs multiple functional units so independent instructions genuinely execute the same cycle rather than merely being fetched together and serialized at execution — often more than one integer ALU, plus separate dedicated units for load/store and branch resolution, since duplicating only ALUs would still bottleneck on memory or branch ops issuing together.

The part that's easy to overlook, and usually the more expensive piece in practice, is the **issue logic**: every cycle, the hardware decides which ready candidate instructions can legally issue together, given dependencies on each other and on available functional units — this gets combinatorially harder as width grows, since dependency-checking scales roughly with the square of issue width. Register file port count also has to grow — a 4-wide machine issuing 4 instructions per cycle needs far more simultaneous ports than a scalar design, and port count is more expensive in area/power than it looks on paper.

**Testing:** naming the concrete duplicated hardware in both front end and back end, and specifically recognizing issue scheduling logic (not just execution units) as a real, superlinear cost.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What superscalar hardware actually adds

interviewQuestions.question: For a beginner: is a superscalar CPU the same thing as a multicore CPU? Both run multiple things at once.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd clarify this distinction directly, since the surface similarity ('multiple things happening simultaneously') hides a genuinely different mechanism underneath.

A superscalar CPU is a **single core** that can issue and execute several instructions from **one instruction stream** in the same cycle — exploiting instruction-level parallelism within one sequential program, entirely invisible to the programmer, who writes ordinary single-threaded code while the hardware finds independence on its own. A multicore CPU has **multiple, physically separate cores**, each an independent processor with its own front end and execution units — running genuinely separate instruction streams (separate threads or processes) that the OS explicitly schedules onto different cores.

Concrete distinction: a single-threaded program that never spawns any additional threads can still benefit from a superscalar core issuing multiple of *its own* independent instructions per cycle — no code change required, since it's entirely a hardware optimization. That same program gets **zero** benefit from having 8 cores available, since it only ever uses one — exploiting multicore requires software explicitly written or compiled to split work across threads.

In practice, virtually every modern CPU core is *both*: a superscalar, out-of-order core repeated across the die as separate cores — the two techniques exploit different sources of parallelism (within one instruction stream vs. across many) and are typically combined, not alternatives.

**Testing:** distinguishing ILP exploited within a single instruction stream from thread/process-level parallelism across cores, and recognizing that real chips combine both rather than choosing one.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Superscalar vs multicore, not the same thing
